right: This is written in docs/docs/Infrastructure/eVault.md, under Rate Limiting. The Registry signs a token for any platform name it is asked for, so the platform name in a token is self-declared: a valid token proves it is genuine, not who sent it. Two things follow. The IP limit is the ceiling: a platform exemption never lets a caller exceed its IP limit, so the first operator should raise or exempt the IPs of that platform's servers as well. And a platform block is advisory, because the blocked caller can simply request a token under another name; the second operator should block its IPs.

## Why it happens

`GlobalRateLimiter` in `infrastructure/evault-core/src/core/http/global-rate-limiter.ts` counts every request against its IP first and only then, if a valid Registry token is attached, against the platform:

```ts
// The Registry signs any platform name, so a platform rule can only narrow
// what a caller may do: nothing a token claims lifts the IP ceiling.
```

The eVault page (Infrastructure/eVault.md, "What a platform rule can and cannot do") gives the reason: the Registry will mint a token for whatever name it is asked for, so the name is only claimed by the caller.

## What to do

- **The exemption**: a platform exemption can never lift a caller above its per-IP limit. Exempt the platform's server IP addresses too, or give them a higher limit.
- **The block**: blocking by name is not durable; the caller just gets a fresh token with a different name. Block the addresses it calls from.

Both come from one fact in the eVault docs: a Registry token's platform field is not verified, because the Registry hands out tokens for any name. So the limiter treats the per-IP budget as the ceiling and a platform rule can only narrow it. To give the busy platform room, add exempt rules (or higher limits) for its servers' IP ranges in the control panel's Rate Limits page. To stop the bad one, block its IP addresses; a name block is advisory, since it can come back under another name.
wrong: Rate-limit rules are only read when evault-core starts, so neither change has taken effect yet. Restart the eVault after adding the exemption and the block and both will apply.

The platform rule is matched exactly against the `platform` value of the token, so the exemption probably has a typo in the subject. The block is probably on the wrong eVault instance; with several instances behind a load balancer each keeps its own rules. Fix the subject name and apply the rule on every instance.

Exemptions only apply to IPs; a platform cannot be exempted at all, and blocked platforms are only refused once their current one-minute window ends. Wait a minute after blocking and the requests will stop.
The eVault rate limiter is fine: a platform exemption is meant to be overridden by the per-minute default, and blocks take up to 30 seconds. Lower the default and wait.

right: All three are explained in docs/docs/W3DS Protocol/Platform-Authentication.md. The issuerJwksUri is supplied by the deployment being checked, so if the verifier fetched keys from it a deployment could point it at a key set it controls and certify itself; instead the certificate's issuer must be on the trusted list (trustedPpaIssuers, by default https://ppa.w3ds.metastate.foundation) and keys come from that issuer's own /.well-known/jwks.json. The challenge is single-use and spent the moment it is answered, whether or not the chain holds, so a captured response cannot be replayed even inside its window. And the deployment presents its evidence rather than being looked up, so the verifier needs only public endpoints and never needs read access to the platform's eVault, which is the very access the deployment is trying to obtain.

## issuerJwksUri

It comes from the deployment, the party under test. Trusting it would let a deployment name its own keys and so sign its own accreditation. `chain.ts` checks `iss` against the trusted PPA list first and then fetches `ppaJwksUri(issuer)`:

```ts
export function ppaJwksUri(issuer: string): string {
	return new URL("/.well-known/jwks.json", issuer).toString();
}
```

## The spent challenge

`createChallengeStore().redeem` deletes the nonce whether the chain then holds or not, so each challenge is used once: a recorded response can't be replayed, and a failed attempt can't be retried with the same nonce.

## No eVault read

PP Auth (W3DS Protocol/Platform-Authentication.md) has the deployment present everything, so a verifier works from public endpoints alone. Reading the platform's eVault would need the access the handshake is meant to grant — it would be circular.

Per the PP Auth page in W3DS Protocol: (1) the evidence's JWKS link is provided by the deployment itself, so honouring it would let it self-certify with its own keys; only trusted issuers' published key sets count. (2) Spending the nonce even on failure makes it single-use, so nobody can replay a captured answer. (3) Evidence is presented, not fetched, so checking needs only public endpoints and no access to the platform's eVault, which is what the deployment is trying to obtain.
wrong: Fetching issuerJwksUri on every handshake would add latency and a network dependency, so the verifier uses a cached copy instead. The challenge is spent to free memory in the challenge store. The verifier doesn't read the eVault because it is faster to check only what is sent.

The issuerJwksUri is ignored because certificates are signed by the Registry, whose JWKS is fixed in the configuration. The nonce is consumed so the same nonce can't be replayed later. And the deployment has no eVault of its own, so there is nothing to read.

issuerJwksUri is legacy: older PPA releases published keys at a different path, and the field is kept for compatibility. The challenge is spent because the verifier keeps no state between requests. The verifier does read the platform's eVault, through the deployment document's binding signatures.
It does all three for performance: remote fetches are slow, stores fill up, and eVault reads are rate limited.

right: These come from docs/docs/W3DS Protocol/Company-Delegation.md. The eVault enforces none of the delegation model: it stores whatever it is given, and all authority is decided by the verifier from signatures and the eVault's version history. Writes are not restricted; a version that is not properly signed is ignored as if absent, so it costs verification time but grants nothing. Because anyone can add versions, a verifier reads at most 2,000 versions of a record, so flooding a record with writes is a denial of service, never a takeover. And a board only counts if the Company record's very first version carries one signed by one of its own directors, so an existing company cannot be claimed by whoever adds directors first.

## Why the eVault accepts the writes

It is not the authority. The verifier works out who may sign from the signatures and the record's history; the vault just stores what it gets.

## Why 2,000 versions

`packages/auth/src/delegated-signature.ts` reads at most `MAX_HISTORY_PAGES` pages of `HISTORY_PAGE` versions:

```ts
const HISTORY_PAGE = 100;
const MAX_HISTORY_PAGES = 20;
```

Anyone can append versions, so this bounds the work: spamming a record can slow verification, but it can never seize authority. Forged or unsigned versions are skipped either way.

## Why the board must be there from the start

If a board could be added later, anyone could take over an existing company by being the first to write directors into it. `resolveBoard` in packages/delegation only accepts a first version that already names directors and is signed by one of them.

Company Delegation (W3DS Protocol) answers all three. 1) The vault doesn't decide anything; verifiers decide from the signatures. Unsigned or forged versions don't count. 2) The 2,000-version cap means flooding is only a DoS. 3) Without it, an existing company could be hijacked by whoever adds directors first.
wrong: The eVault does refuse unauthorised writes: only directors' platforms hold write access to the company vault. The 2,000 cap is a GraphQL pagination limit. A board added later is ignored because Company records are immutable after creation.

Writes are accepted because ACLs on company records are public (`acl: ["*"]`), which is a known gap to be fixed. The verifier stops at 2,000 versions to keep response times under a second. The first version must have directors because the Registry checks it when the company's eVault is provisioned.

The eVault validates every write against the delegation chain before storing it, so the reviewer's worry is unfounded. 2,000 is simply the maximum history the eVault keeps. Boards are fixed at creation because the company's eName is derived from its directors.
It is to keep things simple: the eVault is a dumb store, history is capped for memory, and boards are set once.

right: It is deliberate, and docs/docs/W3DS Protocol/Access-Control.md ("Who the requesting party is") says why. X-ON-BEHALF-OF is an assertion, not a proof: the platform's token does not attest to the user, so the claim is exactly as trustworthy as the platform making it, and the platform can reach what the user was granted, even more than its own grant. That is intended because specificity is what makes a user grant mean anything, and a platform that can write to a vault can already act as its users in other ways. What the header cannot do is escape a denial: denials match the party, the platform carrying the request and the party's groups, so a denied platform stays denied whatever name it puts in the header. Only @-prefixed eNames count as parties; a JWT kid is ignored.

## Not a mistake

This is by design (W3DS Protocol → Access Control, "Who the requesting party is").

`VaultAccessGuard.principalFor` takes the header at the platform's word:

```ts
// The token proves the platform, not the user, so this is the platform's
// assertion and is only as trustworthy as the platform making it.
```

## Why

User grants have to win over platform grants, or a grant to a user would mean nothing; and a platform that can already write to the vault can already act for its users in other ways, so requiring proof here would add little.

## What it cannot do

It can't get past a denial. A denial is matched against the user, the platform carrying the request and the user's groups, so a denied platform is still refused no matter whose eName it sends.

Intentional. The header is the platform's claim, unproven, as trustworthy as the platform itself; the access-control spec accepts that because grant specificity is what makes a user's grant mean anything, and any platform able to write to the vault could already act for its users anyway. But denials still apply: they also match the carrying platform, so the header never lifts a deny.
wrong: Yes, it is a mistake. The eVault should require a wallet signature from the user before honouring X-ON-BEHALF-OF; until then a platform can escalate to any user's permissions. Denials are evaluated after grants, so they do not help.

It is by design because the platform token is a delegation the user signed when they logged in, so the header is proven by the user's own signature. For that reason denials don't apply to calls made for a user.
The header is only used for audit history (the `author` field) and has no effect on access decisions, so there is no hole: access is always decided by the platform's own grant.
It is a known gap: the header is trusted because the Registry vouches for every platform token, and a future version will check it against the user's key binding certificates.
